common_name: October Glory Maple (Late Red Fall-Color Red Maple)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in moist, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; October Glory tolerates wetter soil than many maples and holds its leaves later into fall than most red maple cultivars, giving one of the last big color displays of the season.

directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun, and water deeply and regularly through the first two to three seasons to establish a strong root system before the tree can tolerate occasional dry spells. October Glory is one of the most widely planted red maple cultivars, prized for its dependable, brilliant red-to-scarlet fall color that develops later in the season than most red maple selections, extending fall color displays into late October and November in much of its range. Small red flowers appear on bare branches in late winter, an early sign of spring, followed by summer shade from a dense, rounded to oval canopy. It tolerates a wider range of soil moisture than many shade trees, including occasional wet or poorly drained sites, making it a versatile, fast-growing choice for a lawn specimen or street tree. Prune only to remove dead, damaged, or crossing branches, ideally in late fall or winter to avoid excessive sap bleeding.

common_name: Red Sunset Maple (Early Orange-Red Fall-Color Red Maple)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in moist, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Red Sunset colors earlier in the fall than October Glory, giving gardeners a choice of red maple cultivars to stagger fall color across the landscape.

directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun, watering deeply through establishment to help the root system develop before the tree faces summer heat stress on its own. Red Sunset is a widely planted red maple cultivar selected for its uniform, upright-oval crown and consistently outstanding orange-red fall color, which typically develops earlier in autumn than October Glory, making the two cultivars useful companions for extending a red maple color display across several weeks. Like other red maples, it bears small red flowers on bare branches in late winter and grows at a moderate to fast rate into a dense, symmetrical shade tree well suited to lawns, streets, and parks. It adapts to a range of soil types, including occasional wet conditions, though it performs best with consistent moisture and acidic to neutral soil. Prune to remove dead or crossing branches in late fall or winter dormancy to minimize sap bleeding from cuts.

common_name: Green Giant Arborvitae (Fast-Growing Evergreen Privacy Screen)

planting.note: Plant container trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Green Giant grows quickly, often 3 feet or more per year once established, making it one of the fastest ways to establish a tall evergreen privacy screen.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing trees to allow the dense, pyramidal form to grow together into a solid screen while leaving room for good air circulation. Green Giant is a vigorous hybrid arborvitae, a cross between Western redcedar and Japanese arborvitae, developed for exceptionally fast growth and reliable performance as a large-scale evergreen screen, reaching mature heights of 40–60 feet with a dense, uniform, deep green pyramidal habit that requires little to no shearing to maintain its shape. Unlike Leyland cypress, which has become increasingly prone to canker and root disease problems in the humid Gulf South, Green Giant shows notably better disease resistance and has become the preferred fast-growing screening tree for many Southern landscapes. It tolerates heat, humidity, and a range of soil types once established, and deer browsing is generally minimal compared to other arborvitae. Water deeply and regularly for the first two years to establish a strong root system.

planting.note: Plant container trees in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Leyland cypress is highly prone to Seiridium and Botryosphaeria canker disease in the hot, humid, poorly drained conditions common in the Gulf South, so good drainage, wide spacing for airflow, and avoiding overhead irrigation are essential for long-term success.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, giving trees generous spacing for airflow, since crowding and poor drainage are the leading causes of the canker diseases that shorten this tree's life in humid climates. Leyland cypress is a fast-growing hybrid conifer long popular across the South for quickly establishing a dense, narrow, evergreen privacy screen, capable of adding 3 feet or more of growth per year in its early years to reach a mature height of 40–60 feet with soft, feathery, blue-green foliage. Its rapid growth rate made it the default screening tree for decades, but it is increasingly susceptible to fatal canker diseases in the Gulf South's heat, humidity, and heavy clay soils, particularly when planted too closely together or in poorly drained sites, so many extension services now recommend Green Giant arborvitae or other alternatives for new plantings in this region. Where Leyland cypress is already established or planted with excellent drainage and spacing, minimal pruning is needed beyond an occasional light shearing to maintain shape.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Leyland cypress disease notes

common_name: Autumn Gold Ginkgo (Seedless Male Ginkgo with Golden Fall Color)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; Autumn Gold is a grafted male cultivar selected for a uniform, broadly pyramidal habit and reliable golden fall color, and being male it never produces the malodorous, messy fruit of female ginkgo trees.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun, and water regularly through the first two to three seasons to help the young tree establish, since mature ginkgo are exceptionally tough and drought-, pollution-, and pest-tolerant once rooted in. Autumn Gold is a grafted, male-only selection of ginkgo prized for its symmetrical, broadly pyramidal form and its dependable, uniform display of clear golden-yellow fan-shaped leaves each fall, often dropping in a dramatic, near-simultaneous leaf fall over a day or two once peak color is reached. Because it is propagated from a male tree, Autumn Gold never produces the notoriously foul-smelling, messy fruit that female ginkgo trees bear, making it a far better choice than a seed-grown tree of unknown sex for street tree plantings, lawns, or anywhere fallen fruit would be a nuisance. Ginkgo is one of the most resilient shade trees available, tolerating urban pollution, compacted soil, heat, and periods of drought with ease, and it is essentially free of serious insect and disease problems. Little pruning is needed beyond removing any dead or crossing branches while the tree is young.
